title: Crisis and Renewal
full_title: Plague, Schism and the Fifteenth Century
tagline: Famine, plague, a long war, two popes and then three, humanism as a practice, print, and a year — 1492 — that is asked to mean too much
summary: The fourteenth and fifteenth centuries are not a waiting room for modernity. Plague killed on a scale that has to be stated as a range. The Western Schism and the Hundred Years’ War are political crises with religious and fiscal sides. Humanism is a way of reading and writing. Print is a technology with markets. And 1492 is at least four events.
overview: The Great Famine and the plague of 1347–49 are demographic facts with religious and economic consequences. This atlas does not give a single European death total for the plague. It does say that in many studied regions the estimates lie between about a third and about a half, and that local figures differ.

Two and then three popes, and a war fought at intervals from the conventional date 1337 until Castillon in 1453, belong together as crises of authority and taxation. Joan of Arc is a person inside that war, not a symbol of a nation already formed.

Italian city-states trained humanists to write a classical Latin for chanceries and for fame. Gutenberg’s Bible, about 1454–1455, multiplied a text the Church already held. The fall of Constantinople in May 1453 and the events of 1492 — Granada, the expulsion, Columbus — are contemporaneous with these practices. They do not form one birth of the modern world.
outcomes: State the plague’s arrival and the range of regional estimates without inventing a European total.
Explain the Western Schism and the conventional dates of the Hundred Years’ War as labels as well as conflicts.
Describe humanism as a practice of education and chanceries, not as a personality type.
Say what print changed in the making of books, and what it did not cause by itself.
Separate the events of 1492 into Granada, the Alhambra Decree and Columbus’s voyage.

chapters.title: City-states and humanism
chapters.summary: Italian republics and princes, chancery humanism, and why “the Renaissance” is a label for practices.

history.title: Plague at Messina
history.detail: In October 1347 plague is reported at Messina. It is in much of western Europe in 1348 and 1349. Mortality estimates are regional, not a single European total.

history.title: Two popes
history.detail: The Western Schism begins in 1378 and is ended by the election of Martin V in 1417, after the Council of Constance.

history.title: Constantinople falls
history.detail: On 29 May 1453 Mehmed II takes Constantinople. On 17 July Castillon ends the conventional Hundred Years’ War.

history.title: Four events, one year
history.detail: Granada surrenders on 2 January. The Alhambra Decree is dated 31 March. Columbus sails on 3 August and makes landfall on 12 October.

references.title: The Black Death
references.note: A collection of sources, so the mortality is read from witnesses rather than from a single modern total.

references.title: The Hundred Years War
references.note: The wars of 1337–1453 as politics, taxation and society, not as one battle.

references.title: The Renaissance in Italy: A Social and Cultural History
references.note: Humanism and the arts inside Italian society, not as a mood that floated over it.

references.title: 1492: The Year Our World Began
references.note: A world history of the year, useful here as a warning against letting one landfall stand for all of it.
